column2: From Abū Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him) that the Prophet ﷺ said: “Part of the excellence of a person's Islam is his leaving what does not concern him.” A good (ḥasan) hadith, reported by al-Tirmidhī and others.

Al-Tirmidhī and Ibn Mājah recorded this hadith in the narration of al-Awzāʿī, from Qurrah ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, from al-Zuhrī, from Abū Salamah, from Abū Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with them). Al-Tirmidhī said: unusual (gharīb). The Shaykh, the compiler (may Allah have mercy on him), graded it good,

because the men of its chain are reliable. Qurrah ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Ḥaywīl was declared reliable by some and weak by others. Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr said: This hadith is preserved from al-Zuhrī with this chain in the narration of reliable narrators;
and this accords with the Shaykh's grading of it as good. Most of the imams, however, said that it is not preserved with this chain; it is preserved only from al-Zuhrī, from ʿAlī ibn Ḥusayn,
from the Prophet ﷺ, as a mursal report. That is how the reliable narrators narrated it from al-Zuhrī, among them Mālik in the Muwaṭṭaʾ, Yūnus, Maʿmar and Ibrāhīm ibn Saʿd — except that Ibrāhīm said:
“Part of a person's faith is his leaving what does not concern him.” Among those who said that it is authentic only from ʿAlī ibn Ḥusayn as a mursal report are Imam Aḥmad, Yaḥyā ibn Maʿīn,

al-Bukhārī and al-Dāraquṭnī. Weak narrators confused its chain from al-Zuhrī outrageously, and what is correct is the mursal version. ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿUmar al-ʿUmarī narrated it from al-Zuhrī, from ʿAlī ibn Ḥusayn,
from his father, from the Prophet ﷺ, thus making it connected and placing it among the hadiths of al-Ḥusayn ibn ʿAlī; Imam Aḥmad recorded it in his Musnad by this route.
But al-ʿUmarī is not a ḥāfiẓ. Aḥmad also recorded it by another route from al-Ḥusayn, from the Prophet ﷺ, and al-Bukhārī declared it weak by this route too in his Tārīkh,
saying: It is authentic only from ʿAlī ibn Ḥusayn as a mursal report. It has also been narrated from the Prophet ﷺ by other routes, all of them weak.

This hadith is one of the great foundations of good conduct (adab). Imam Abū ʿAmr ibn al-Ṣalāḥ reported that Abū Muḥammad ibn Abī Zayd, the imam of the Mālikīs in his time, said: The whole of good manners, and the reins that govern them, branch out from four hadiths:
The words of the Prophet ﷺ, “Whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day should speak good or keep silent”; his words ﷺ,

“Part of the excellence of a person's Islam is his leaving what does not concern him”; his words to the man for whom he kept his counsel brief, “Do not become angry”; and his words ﷺ, “The believer loves for his brother what he loves for himself.”
The meaning of this hadith is that part of the excellence of a person's Islam is leaving whatever words and deeds do not concern him, and confining himself to the words and deeds that do concern him.

“What concerns him” (yaʿnīhi) means what his concern (ʿināyah) attaches to, what he aims at and seeks. ʿInāyah is intense concern for something; one says ʿanāhu yaʿnīhi when one is concerned with something and seeks it.

What is meant is not that he leaves what he has no concern for and no wish for at the dictate of desire and the soul's wants, but at the dictate of the Sharīʿah and of Islam. That is why he made it part of the excellence of Islam.

When a person's Islam is excellent, he leaves whatever words and deeds do not concern him in Islam. For Islam requires doing what is obligatory, as was mentioned in the commentary on the hadith of Jibrīl (peace be upon him).

Complete, praiseworthy Islam, moreover, includes leaving forbidden things, as he ﷺ said: “The Muslim is the one from whose tongue and hand the Muslims are safe.” When Islam is excellent, it requires leaving everything that does not concern one — forbidden things, doubtful things, disliked things

and superfluous permissible things that are not needed. For none of this concerns the Muslim once his Islam is complete and he has reached the degree of iḥsān, which is to worship Allah the Exalted as though he sees Him — and if he does not see Him, Allah sees him.

Whoever worships Allah keeping present in his heart His nearness and the sense of witnessing Him, or keeping present Allah's nearness to him and His watching over him, has excellent Islam; and it follows from this that he leaves everything that does not concern him in Islam and occupies himself with what does concern him in it.

For from these two stations arise modesty before Allah and the leaving of everything one would be ashamed of, just as he ﷺ advised a man to be as modest before Allah as he would be before a righteous man of his clan who never left his side.

In the Musnad and in al-Tirmidhī, from Ibn Masʿūd, as marfūʿ (the Prophet's words): “Modesty before Allah the Exalted is that you guard the head and what it holds, guard the belly and what it contains, and remember death and decay. Whoever does that has been modest before Allah as modesty truly requires.”
One of them said: Be modest before Allah in proportion to His nearness to you, and fear Allah in proportion to His power over you.
One of those who know Allah said: When you speak, remember that Allah hears you; and when you are silent, remember that He sees you.
This meaning is pointed to in the Mighty Qurʾān in many places, such as His words, the Exalted:

“We created man and We know what his soul whispers to him, and We are nearer to him than his jugular vein, when the two receivers receive, seated on the right and on the left. He utters not a word but there is a watcher by him, ready” [Qāf 50:16–18]; and His words, the Exalted:

“You are not engaged in any matter, nor do you recite any of the Qurʾān, nor do you do any deed, but We are witnesses over you when you are engaged in it. Not an atom's weight in the earth or in the heaven escapes your Lord, nor anything smaller than that or greater, but it is in a clear Book” [Yūnus 10:61];
and the Exalted said: “Or do they think that We do not hear their secrets and their private talk? Indeed We do, and Our messengers are with them, writing” [al-Zukhruf 43:80].
What is mostly meant by leaving what does not concern one is guarding the tongue from idle talk, as the first verses quoted, from Sūrat Qāf, indicate.
In the Musnad, from the hadith of al-Ḥusayn, the Prophet ﷺ said: “Part of the excellence of a person's Islam is speaking little about what does not concern him.”
Al-Kharāʾiṭī recorded from the hadith of Ibn Masʿūd, who said: A man came to the Prophet ﷺ and said:
O Messenger of Allah, I am obeyed among my people; what should I command them to do?
He said to him: “Command them to spread the greeting of peace, and to speak little except about what concerns them.”
In Ṣaḥīḥ Ibn Ḥibbān, from Abū Dharr, the Prophet ﷺ said: “In the scrolls of Ibrāhīm (blessings and peace be upon him) it was written:

The intelligent man, so long as his reason is not overcome, should have hours: an hour in which he converses intimately with his Lord, an hour in which he takes himself to account, an hour in which he reflects on what Allah has made,

and an hour in which he is free for his needs of food and drink. The intelligent man should not travel except for one of three things: provision for the Return, the upkeep of his livelihood, or enjoyment of what is not forbidden.
The intelligent man should have insight into his times, attend to his own affairs and guard his tongue. Whoever counts his speech as part of his deeds speaks little, except about what concerns him.”
ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz (may Allah have mercy on him) said: Whoever counts his speech as part of his deeds speaks little, except about what concerns him.
It is as he said,

for many people do not count their speech as part of their deeds, and so they speak recklessly and without care. This was hidden even from Muʿādh ibn Jabal, so that he asked the Prophet ﷺ about it: Will we be taken to account for what we say?
He said: “May your mother be bereft of you, Muʿādh! Is there anything that throws people on their faces in the Fire but the harvests of their tongues?”

Allah has denied that there is any good in much of what people say to one another in private, saying: “There is no good in much of their private talk, except for one who enjoins charity, or what is right, or making peace between people” [al-Nisāʾ 4:114].

Al-Tirmidhī and Ibn Mājah recorded from the hadith of Umm Ḥabībah that the Prophet ﷺ said: “All the speech of the son of Ādam counts against him, not for him, except commanding right, forbidding wrong and the remembrance of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.”

Some people expressed surprise at this hadith in the presence of Sufyān al-Thawrī, and Sufyān said: Why does this surprise you? Has Allah the Exalted not said: “There is no good in much of their private talk, except for one who enjoins charity, or what is right, or making peace between people”?
Has the Exalted not said: “The Day the Spirit and the angels stand in rows, they will not speak, except one whom the All-Merciful permits and who says what is right” [al-Nabaʾ 78:38]?
Al-Tirmidhī recorded from the hadith of Anas, who said: A man of his Companions — meaning the Prophet's ﷺ — died, and a man said: Rejoice in the good news of Paradise!
The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: “Do you not know? Perhaps he spoke about what did not concern him, or was miserly with what could not have made him rich.”
The meaning of this hadith has been narrated from the Prophet ﷺ by several routes, and some of them state that the man had been killed as a martyr.

Abū al-Qāsim al-Baghawī recorded in his Muʿjam, from the hadith of Shihāb ibn Mālik, who had come in a delegation to the Prophet ﷺ, that he heard the Prophet ﷺ when a woman said to him: O Messenger of Allah, will you not greet us?
He said: “You are of a group of women who make little of much, who withhold what would not make them rich, and who ask about what does not concern them.”
Al-ʿUqaylī recorded from the hadith of Abū Hurayrah, as marfūʿ: “The people with the most sins are those who talk most about what does not concern them.”
ʿAmr ibn Qays al-Mulāʾī said: A man passed by Luqmān while people were gathered around him, and said to him: Are you not the slave of the tribe of so-and-so?
He said: Yes. He said: The one who used to herd sheep by such-and-such a mountain?
He said: Yes. He said: Then what has brought you to what I see?
He said: Truthful speech, and long silence about what does not concern me.

Wahb ibn Munabbih said: Among the Children of Israel there were two men whose worship brought them to the point of walking on water. While they were walking on the sea, they came upon a man walking on the air. They said to him: O servant of Allah, by what did you attain this rank?

He said: By a small portion of this world: I weaned my soul from its desires, held back my tongue from what does not concern me, desired what He called me to, and kept to silence. If I swear by Allah, He fulfils my oath, and if I ask Him, He gives to me.

People visited one of the Companions in his illness, and his face was shining. They asked him why his face was shining, and he said: There is no deed of mine I rely on more than two qualities: I did not speak about what did not concern me, and my heart was free of ill will towards the Muslims.
Muwarriq al-ʿIjlī said: There is something I have been seeking for so many years; I have not managed it, and I will never give up seeking it. They said: What is it?
He said: Refraining from what does not concern me.
Ibn Abī al-Dunyā narrated it.

Asad ibn Mūsā narrated: Abū Maʿshar told us, from Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: “The first to come in to you will be a man of the people of Paradise.” Then ʿAbdullāh ibn Salām came in.

Some people went up to him and told him, and said to him: Tell us which of your deeds you rely on most. He said: My deeds are weak; what I rely on most, in hope, is soundness of heart and my leaving what does not concern me.
Abū ʿUbaydah narrated that al-Ḥasan said: One of the signs that Allah the Exalted has turned away from a servant is that He makes him busy with what does not concern him.

Sahl ibn ʿAbdullāh al-Tustarī said: Whoever talks about what does not concern him is deprived of truthfulness. Maʿrūf said: A servant's talking about what does not concern him is Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, forsaking him.

This hadith shows that leaving what does not concern a person is part of the excellence of his Islam. When he leaves what does not concern him and does everything that does concern him, the excellence of his Islam is complete. Hadiths have come about the merit of one whose Islam is excellent: that his good deeds are multiplied and his evil deeds expiated.

It appears that the degree of multiplication depends on how excellent one's Islam is. In Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, from Abū Hurayrah, the Prophet ﷺ said: “When one of you makes his Islam excellent, every good deed he does is written for him as ten like it, up to seven hundred times,

and every evil deed he does is written as one like it, until he meets Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.” The tenfold multiplication of a good deed is certain; the increase beyond that depends on the excellence of one's Islam, the sincerity of one's intention, and the need for that deed and its merit — such as spending in jihād,

in Ḥajj, on relatives, on orphans and the poor, and at times when spending is needed. This is supported by what is narrated from ʿAṭiyyah, from Ibn ʿUmar, who said: “Whoever brings a good deed will have ten like it” [al-Anʿām 6:160] was revealed about the Bedouins. He was asked: Then what do the Emigrants have?
He said: Something more than that. Then he recited His words, the Exalted: “And if there is a good deed, He multiplies it and gives from His own presence a great reward” [al-Nisāʾ 4:40].
Al-Nasāʾī recorded from the hadith of Abū Saʿīd that the Prophet ﷺ said: “When a servant becomes Muslim and his Islam is excellent, Allah records for him every good deed he had done before,

and every evil deed he had done before is erased from him. After that comes the reckoning: a good deed is ten like it, up to seven hundred times, and an evil deed is one like it, unless Allah pardons it.” In another narration: “And he is told: Begin your deeds afresh.”

What is meant by the good and evil deeds he had done before is what he did before Islam. This shows that he is rewarded for the good deeds he did as a disbeliever once he becomes Muslim, and that his evil deeds are erased once he becomes Muslim — but on condition that his Islam is excellent

and that he guards against those evil deeds while in Islam. Imam Aḥmad stated this explicitly. It is shown by what is in the two Ṣaḥīḥs from Ibn Masʿūd, who said: We said: O Messenger of Allah, will we be taken to account for what we did in the Jāhiliyyah?
He said: “Whoever among you does well in Islam will not be taken to account for it; and whoever does ill will be taken to account for his deeds in the Jāhiliyyah and in Islam.”
In Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀṣ said to the Prophet ﷺ when he became Muslim: I want to make a condition. He said: “What condition?”
I said: That I be forgiven. He said: “Do you not know that Islam demolishes what came before it?”

Imam Aḥmad recorded it, and his wording is: “Islam cuts off the sins that came before it.” This is to be understood as referring to complete and excellent Islam, so as to reconcile it with the hadith of Ibn Masʿūd before it.
Also in Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, Ḥakīm ibn Ḥizām said: I said: O Messenger of Allah, what of things I used to do in the Jāhiliyyah — charity, freeing slaves or keeping ties of kinship — is there reward in them?
The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: “You have become Muslim along with the good you did before.” In another of Muslim's narrations he said: I said:

By Allah, I will not leave anything I did in the Jāhiliyyah without doing the like of it in Islam. This shows that a disbeliever is rewarded for his good deeds when he becomes Muslim, as the hadith of Abū Saʿīd quoted above also shows.
It has been said that his evil deeds from the time of shirk are turned into good deeds and that he is rewarded for them, taking this from His words, the Exalted:

“And those who do not call on another god along with Allah, nor kill the soul Allah has made sacred except by right, nor commit fornication — whoever does that will meet the penalty: the punishment will be doubled for him on the Day of Resurrection, and he will abide in it humiliated — except for those who repent, believe and do righteous deeds; for them Allah will replace their evil deeds with good deeds” [al-Furqān 25:68–70].
The Qurʾān commentators have differed about this replacement, holding two views.
Some said it is in this world, meaning that for whoever becomes Muslim and repents to Him, Allah replaces the disbelief and sins he was in with faith and righteous deeds.

Ibrāhīm al-Ḥarbī reported this view in Gharīb al-Ḥadīth from most of the commentators, naming among them Ibn ʿAbbās, ʿAṭāʾ, Qatādah, al-Suddī and ʿIkrimah. I say: It is also the well-known view of al-Ḥasan.
He said: Al-Ḥasan, Abū Mālik and others said: It concerns the people of shirk specifically, not the people of Islam.
I say: This view is sound only if the replacement is in the Hereafter, as will be discussed below. If it is said to be in this world,
then a disbeliever who becomes Muslim and a Muslim who repents are alike in this; indeed, the Muslim who repents is in a better state than the disbeliever who becomes Muslim.

He said: Others said that the replacement is in the Hereafter: in place of every evil deed they are given a good deed. Among them are ʿAmr ibn Maymūn, Makḥūl, Ibn al-Musayyib and ʿAlī ibn al-Ḥusayn. He said: Abū al-ʿĀliyah, Mujāhid

and Khālid Sabalān rejected it, and it is open to objection on several points. Then he mentioned, in substance, that it would follow that someone with many evil deeds would be better off than someone with few, since he would be given a good deed in place of every evil deed.

Then he said: If someone said that Allah only mentioned that He replaces evil deeds with good deeds and did not mention the number — how they are replaced — it would be possible that the meaning of replacement is

that someone who committed a single evil deed and repented of it has it replaced with a hundred thousand good deeds, and that someone who committed a thousand evil deeds has them replaced with a thousand good deeds; in that case the one with fewer evil deeds would be better off.
I say: This view — that the replacement is in the Hereafter — was rejected by Abū al-ʿĀliyah, who recited His words, the Exalted:

“The Day every soul will find what it has done of good brought before it, and what it has done of evil it will wish there were a great distance between itself and it” [Āl ʿImrān 3:30]. Some refuted it with His words, the Exalted:
“And whoever does an atom's weight of evil will see it” [al-Zalzalah 99:8], and His words, the Exalted:

“And the Book will be placed, and you will see the criminals fearful of what is in it, saying: ‘Woe to us! What is this Book that leaves out nothing small or great without counting it?’ They will find what they did present before them, and your Lord wrongs no one” [al-Kahf 18:49]. But the reply has been given that the repentant is made to stand before his evil deeds

and then they are turned into good deeds. Abū ʿUthmān al-Nahdī said: The believer is given his book under a veil from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. He reads his evil deeds, and as he reads them his colour changes, until he passes on to his good deeds; he reads them and his colour returns to him.

Then he looks, and lo, his evil deeds have been turned into good deeds. At that he says: “Here, read my book!” [al-Ḥāqqah 69:19]. Some narrated this from Abū ʿUthmān, from Ibn Masʿūd, and others from Abū ʿUthmān, from Salmān.
In Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, from the hadith of Abū Dharr, the Prophet ﷺ said: “I know the last of the people of Paradise to enter Paradise, and the last of the people of the Fire to come out of it:

a man brought forward on the Day of Resurrection, and it is said: Show him his small sins and keep his great ones away from him. So Allah shows him his small sins, and he is told: On such-and-such a day you did such-and-such,
and on such-and-such a day you did such-and-such. He says: Yes — he cannot deny it, and he is afraid that his great sins will be shown to him. Then he is told:
In place of every evil deed you have a good deed. He says: My Lord, I did things I do not see here.” He said: And I saw the Messenger of Allah ﷺ laugh until his molar teeth showed.
If evil deeds are replaced with good deeds for someone who was punished in the Fire for his sins, then all the more so for someone whose evil deeds were erased by Islam and sincere repentance,
because erasing them in that way is more beloved to Allah than erasing them through punishment.

Al-Ḥākim recorded, by way of al-Faḍl ibn Mūsā, from Abū al-ʿAnbas, from his father, from Abū Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: “Some people will wish that they had committed more evil deeds.” They said: Why, O Messenger of Allah?
He said: “They are those whose evil deeds Allah has replaced with good deeds.” Ibn Abī Ḥātim recorded it by way of Sulaymān Abū Dāwūd al-Zuhrī, from Abū al-ʿAnbas, from his father,

from Abū Hurayrah as mawqūf (his own words), which is more likely than the marfūʿ version. Something similar is also narrated from al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī, contrary to his well-known view that the replacement is in this world.

As for what al-Ḥarbī said about the replacement — that the good deeds of someone with few evil deeds are increased and those of someone with many evil deeds are reduced — the hadith of Abū Dharr explicitly refutes this: he is given a good deed in place of every evil deed.

As for his saying that it would follow that someone with many evil deeds would be better off than someone with few, the reply is that the replacement applies only to someone who regrets his evil deeds

and keeps them before his eyes, so that every time he remembers them his fear, dread and shame before Allah increase, and so does his haste to do the righteous deeds that expiate them, as the Exalted said:
“except for those who repent, believe and do righteous deeds” [al-Furqān 25:70]. All that we have mentioned falls under righteous deeds. Whoever is in this state

swallows of the bitterness of regret and sorrow for his sins many times what he tasted of their sweetness when he committed them, and each of his sins becomes the cause of righteous deeds that erase it. After this, it is not to be thought strange that these sins should be turned into good deeds.

Explicit hadiths have come stating that when a disbeliever becomes Muslim and his Islam is excellent, his evil deeds from the time of shirk are turned into good deeds. Al-Ṭabarānī recorded from the hadith of ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Jubayr ibn Nufayr,

from Abū Farwah Shaṭb, that he came to the Prophet ﷺ and said: What do you think of a man who has committed every sin and left nothing undone, small or great — is there any repentance for him? He said: “Have you become Muslim?”
He said: Yes. He said: “Then do good deeds and leave evil deeds, and Allah will make them all good deeds for you.” He said: And my acts of treachery and my debaucheries?
He said: “Yes.” The narrator said: He kept saying “Allāhu akbar” until he passed out of sight.
He also recorded it by another route, with a weak chain, from Salamah ibn Nufayl, from the Prophet ﷺ.

Ibn Abī Ḥātim recorded something similar from the hadith of Makḥūl as a mursal report. Al-Bazzār recorded the first hadith, and his version has: from Abū Ṭawīl Shaṭb al-Mamdūd, that he came to the Prophet ﷺ — and he mentioned it with the same meaning. Abū al-Qāsim al-Baghawī likewise recorded it in his Muʿjam,

and said that the correct version is from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Jubayr ibn Nufayr as a mursal report: that a man who was ṭawīl shaṭb [tall and lanky] came to the Prophet ﷺ — shaṭb in the language meaning “long, drawn out” — and one of the narrators misread it and took it for a man's name.
